questions.stem: Which statement describes a trading business?
options: It cannot sell its goods to customers on credit
It buys goods and resells them to earn a profit
It earns its revenue mainly by providing services
It records inventory only once it has been paid for
questions.explanation: A trading business buys inventory and sells it at a higher price, earning gross profit. A service business earns fees for work instead, and trading businesses commonly sell on credit.

questions.stem: For a trading business, Cost of Goods Sold is:
options: the selling price of the inventory sold during the period
the cost of all the inventory purchased during the period
the cost of the inventory still on hand at the period end
the cost price of the inventory sold during the period
questions.explanation: Cost of Goods Sold is an expense equal to the cost of the goods that were actually sold. Goods bought but not yet sold remain in the Inventory asset, so total purchases are not the expense.

questions.stem: Spoke & Chain imports bicycles. For each bike it pays a purchase price of $400, freight to its shop of $30, import duty of $20 and GST of $45. What cost price per bike is entered on the inventory card?
questions.explanation: Cost price includes all costs of getting the goods to the shop ready for sale: $400 + $30 + $20 = $450. GST is excluded because the business claims it back as a GST credit, so $495 overstates the cost.

questions.stem: GST paid on purchases of inventory is excluded from the cost price of the inventory because:
options: it is claimed back from the ATO as a credit
it is recorded as an expense when it is paid
it is reported as Cost of Goods Sold when sold
it is treated as drawings made by the owner
questions.explanation: The business can claim the GST it pays on inventory from the ATO, so it is not part of what the goods cost. It is debited to GST Clearing, not to any expense.

questions.stem: Which of the following costs is excluded from the cost price of inventory?
options: Customs duty paid on imported goods
Insurance on goods in transit to the store
Freight paid to deliver goods to customers
Freight paid to bring goods from the supplier
questions.explanation: Cost price includes the costs of getting goods into the business ready for sale, such as freight in, customs duty and insurance in transit. Delivering goods to customers happens after the goods are ready for sale, so it is a selling expense.

questions.stem: The First-In, First-Out (FIFO) method assumes that:
options: all items are valued at their average cost price
the first items bought are the first items sold
the last items purchased are the first items sold
every item's actual cost is tracked individually
questions.explanation: FIFO assumes the oldest inventory leaves first, so cost of goods sold uses the oldest cost prices and closing inventory uses the latest. Tracking each item's own cost is the Identified Cost method.

questions.stem: A kitchenware store's inventory card shows a balance of 10 kettles at $20. It buys 20 more at $22, then sells 15. Using FIFO, what is the cost of goods sold?
questions.explanation: FIFO takes the oldest cost first: 10 × $20 + 5 × $22 = $200 + $110 = $310. Costing all 15 at $22 gives $330, and an average cost of about $21.33 gives $320.

questions.stem: The store sold 15 kettles: 10 at a cost of $20 and then 5 at $22. A customer returns 2 kettles. Under the study design's FIFO convention, at what cost are they returned to the inventory card?
options: $50 (2 at the $25 selling price)
questions.explanation: For sales returns the study design uses the latest cost prices in the OUT column, reversing the last out, so the 2 kettles are costed at $22 each. Using the oldest price of $20 applies the inventory loss rule, not the sales return rule.

questions.stem: An inventory card shows 8 units at $15 (older) and 12 units at $18. A physical count finds 17 units on hand. Under FIFO, a loss is valued at the oldest cost of inventory on hand. What is the inventory loss?
questions.explanation: Three units are missing. The study design values an inventory loss using the oldest cost price of the inventory on hand on the inventory card, so the loss is 3 × $15 = $45. Using the latest cost price gives $54, which is the rule for inventory gains.

questions.stem: A stocktake at a toy shop finds 18 puzzles on the shelves, although the FIFO inventory card shows 16: 6 bought at $30 and then 10 bought at $34. At what amount is the inventory gain recorded?
questions.explanation: There are 2 more units than recorded. The study design values a FIFO inventory gain at the latest cost price in the IN column, so the gain is 2 × $34 = $68. Using the oldest price of $30 gives $60, the rule for losses rather than gains.

questions.stem: Under both FIFO and Identified Cost, inventory returned to a supplier is recorded at:
options: the latest cost price shown in the OUT column
the selling price the business charges customers
the cost price on the supplier's credit note
the oldest cost price shown on the inventory card
questions.explanation: The supplier's credit note states the cost of the goods being returned, so that is the cost recorded. The latest OUT cost is the FIFO rule for goods returned by customers.

questions.stem: When purchase prices have been rising, the closing inventory on a FIFO inventory card is valued at:
options: the current selling prices of the goods
the most recent, higher cost prices
the oldest, lower cost prices
the average of all cost prices paid
questions.explanation: Because FIFO sends the oldest units out first, the units left are the most recently purchased, at the latest prices. The older, cheaper costs have already gone to Cost of Goods Sold.

questions.stem: The owner of a homewares shop takes 3 lamps home for personal use. How is this recorded?
options: At selling price as Sales revenue
At cost price as Cost of Goods Sold
At selling price as Drawings, reducing Inventory
At cost price as Drawings, reducing Inventory
questions.explanation: Drawings of inventory are recorded at cost price, with GST excluded, and reduce both Inventory and owner's equity. No sale has occurred, so there is no revenue or Cost of Goods Sold.

questions.stem: A sports store gives away inventory that cost $120 as prizes in a competition to promote the store. How is this recorded?
options: Advertising expense of $120, reducing Inventory
Cost of Goods Sold of $120, reducing Inventory
Drawings of $120, reducing owner's equity
Sales revenue at the goods' selling price
questions.explanation: Inventory used for advertising becomes an Advertising expense at its cost price, with GST excluded. It is not Cost of Goods Sold because no sale took place, and the owner did not take it for private use.

questions.stem: Under the Identified Cost method, the cost of goods sold for an item is:
options: the actual cost of the particular item sold
the cost of the oldest items held in inventory
the cost of the most recent purchase of the item
the average cost of all the items held in inventory
questions.explanation: Identified Cost tracks each item, so the cost recorded is that item's own cost from the documents or inventory card. Taking the oldest cost first is FIFO.

questions.stem: Which type of inventory is best suited to the Identified Cost method?
options: Bottled water, with identical bottles bought in bulk each week
Packets of screws, sold in large numbers every single day
Loaves of bread, with fresh identical deliveries each morning
Used cars, each with its own cost and identification number
questions.explanation: Identified Cost suits high-value items that can each be told apart, such as cars with identification numbers. Large volumes of identical, low-cost items are impractical to track one by one, so FIFO suits them.

questions.stem: Riverside Motors holds three cars costing $12,000 (car A, bought first), $15,000 (car B) and $18,000 (car C). It sells car B for $21,000 (excluding GST). Using Identified Cost, what is the gross profit on the sale?
questions.explanation: Identified Cost uses the cost of the car actually sold: $21,000 − $15,000 = $6,000. Using car A's cost, as FIFO would, gives $9,000, but this business identifies each car.

questions.stem: Under the Identified Cost method, an inventory loss is determined by:
options: valuing the missing items at the latest cost price in the IN column
estimating the loss from the business's usual gross profit margin
a physical count that reveals which items, at which costs, are missing
assuming the items lost were those with the oldest cost prices
questions.explanation: Because each item is identified, a physical count shows exactly which items are missing and what each cost. The oldest cost rule applies only to FIFO.

questions.stem: The study design values a FIFO inventory gain at the latest cost price in the IN column. Which qualitative characteristic does it link this to?
options: Understandability
Faithful representation
Comparability
Timeliness
questions.explanation: Using the latest cost price gives a value closest to what the extra goods are really worth to the business, which the study design links to faithful representation. Timeliness concerns when information is available, not how it is valued.

questions.stem: Recording inventory taken by the owner as Drawings rather than as a business expense applies which accounting assumption?
options: Accrual basis
Accounting entity
Going concern
Period
questions.explanation: The owner's private use of goods is a personal transaction, so the entity assumption keeps it out of the business's expenses. Recording it as an expense would understate the business's profit.

questions.stem: A business has always used FIFO. Its owner suggests switching each year to whichever method gives the higher profit. Which qualitative characteristic would this most clearly undermine?
options: Understandability
Verifiability
Comparability
Timeliness
questions.explanation: Changing methods from year to year means differences in profit may come from the method, not from performance, so results cannot be compared over time. The figures could still be on time, clear and supported by documents.

questions.stem: A business returns faulty goods to its supplier. Which source document confirms the cost of the return?
options: The statement of account sent to customers
The credit note received from the supplier
The sales invoice issued to the supplier
The delivery docket received from the supplier
questions.explanation: The supplier issues a credit note that reduces the amount owed and states the cost of the goods returned. A delivery docket comes with goods when they arrive, not when they are sent back.

questions.stem: Before recording a purchase, a store checks the goods that arrived against the order and the document that came with the delivery. Which document lists the goods delivered?
options: The bank statement
The cash receipt
The delivery docket
The credit note
questions.explanation: The delivery docket lists what was delivered, so it can be checked against the order and the purchase invoice before payment. This internal control ensures the business pays only for goods it actually received.

questions.stem: A business had inventory of $16,000 at the start of the year and $20,000 at the end. Its cost of goods sold for the year was $73,000. What is its inventory turnover?
options: 90 days
100 days
80 days
180 days
questions.explanation: Average inventory = (16,000 + 20,000) ÷ 2 = $18,000, and inventory turnover = 18,000 × 365 ÷ 73,000 = 90 days. Using only closing inventory gives 100 days, and forgetting to halve the total gives 180 days.

questions.stem: A shop's inventory turnover rose from 45 days to 60 days. This means:
options: the shop is paying its suppliers more slowly
gross profit must have increased over the year
inventory is taking longer to sell, so turnover is slower
inventory is selling more quickly, which is an improvement
questions.explanation: Inventory turnover measures the average number of days inventory is held before it is sold, so more days means slower selling. How quickly suppliers are paid is measured by accounts payable turnover.

questions.stem: Which action is most likely to slow a business's inventory turnover?
options: Ordering smaller quantities of inventory more often
Dropping product lines that rarely sell to customers
Buying a large quantity of a slow-selling product
Running a clearance sale to sell off old inventory
questions.explanation: Large amounts of slow-selling goods raise average inventory without raising cost of goods sold by as much, so the days held increase. The other actions reduce average inventory or clear old goods, which speeds turnover.

questions.stem: A trading business sells goods on credit for $550 including GST. The goods cost $300. Which amounts are recorded in the Sales Journal?
options: Accounts Receivable $550, Sales $500, GST $50, Cost of Goods Sold $330
Accounts Receivable $550, Sales $500, GST $50, Cost of Goods Sold $300
Accounts Receivable $550, Sales $550, GST $0, Cost of Goods Sold $300
Accounts Receivable $500, Sales $500, GST $50, Cost of Goods Sold $300
questions.explanation: The customer owes the GST-inclusive $550, which splits into Sales of $500 and GST of $50. The cost column records the $300 cost price, which excludes GST, so $330 is wrong.

questions.stem: A business buys inventory and pays immediately by EFT. Where is this recorded?
options: The Purchases Journal, in the Accounts Payable column
The Cash Payments Journal, in the Inventory column
The Purchases Journal, in the Inventory column
The Cash Payments Journal, in the Cost of Goods Sold column
questions.explanation: A purchase paid for at once is a cash payment, so it goes in the Cash Payments Journal, and the goods are added to Inventory at cost. The Purchases Journal is only for credit purchases.

questions.stem: A credit purchase of inventory for $3,300 including GST is recorded in the Purchases Journal. Which amounts are entered?
options: Cost of Goods Sold $3,000, GST $300, Accounts Payable $3,300
Inventory $2,970, GST $330, Accounts Payable $3,300
Inventory $3,000, GST $300, Accounts Payable $3,300
Inventory $3,300, GST $300, Accounts Payable $3,600
questions.explanation: The supplier is owed the full $3,300, of which one-eleventh, $300, is GST and $3,000 is the cost of the inventory. Goods are recorded as Inventory when bought and become Cost of Goods Sold only when sold.

questions.stem: Inventory on hand at the end of the reporting period is reported as:
options: an investing outflow in the Cash Flow Statement
a current asset in the Balance Sheet
a non-current asset in the Balance Sheet
an expense in the Income Statement
questions.explanation: Inventory is held for sale and expected to be sold within 12 months, so it is a current asset. It becomes an expense, Cost of Goods Sold, only when it is sold.

questions.stem: Payments to suppliers for inventory are reported in the Cash Flow Statement under:
options: financing activities
non-current assets
operating activities
investing activities
questions.explanation: Buying inventory is part of the day-to-day trading of the business, so it is an operating activity. Investing activities are for non-current assets, which inventory is not.

questions.stem: For the year, a business had sales of $120,000, sales returns of $5,000 and cost of goods sold of $69,000. What is its gross profit?
questions.explanation: Net sales = 120,000 − 5,000 = $115,000, and gross profit = 115,000 − 69,000 = $46,000. Ignoring the returns gives $51,000, and $115,000 is net sales, not gross profit.

questions.stem: A business fails to record an inventory loss revealed by its physical count. What is the effect on its reports?
options: Cash at bank and net profit are both overstated
Inventory and net profit are both overstated
Inventory is overstated and net profit is understated
Inventory is understated and net profit is overstated
questions.explanation: The missing goods are still shown as Inventory, so the asset is overstated, and the Inventory Loss expense is left out, so profit is overstated. No cash is involved in an inventory loss, so cash is unaffected.

questions.stem: A business budgets for cost of goods sold of $60,000 next year. Inventory is expected to be $15,000 at the start of the year, and the owner wants $18,000 on hand at the end. What are its budgeted purchases of inventory?
questions.explanation: Purchases must cover the goods to be sold plus the increase in inventory: 60,000 + 18,000 − 15,000 = $63,000. Subtracting the increase instead of adding it gives $57,000.

questions.stem: A budgeted Income Statement differs from a historical Income Statement because it:
options: is prepared after the period, using the actual results
shows the assets and liabilities at a particular date
estimates the revenue and expenses for a future period
reports only the cash received and paid by the business
questions.explanation: A budget is a forecast for a coming period, used for planning and later compared with actual results. A historical report records what actually happened.

questions.stem: Inventory rotation means:
options: selling older items before newer ones to reduce spoilage and obsolescence
moving inventory between the business's store locations each month
replacing the entire product range at the start of each season
counting a different section of the inventory every week of the year
questions.explanation: Rotation puts older stock at the front so it sells first, reducing goods that expire or go out of date. It is a physical handling practice, separate from the cost assignment method used on inventory cards.

questions.stem: A business sets a minimum inventory level for each product and reorders when it is reached. What is the main benefit?
options: It removes the need for regular physical counts of inventory
It guarantees the business a faster inventory turnover
It raises the mark-up the business can add to each product
It reduces the risk of running out of stock and losing sales
questions.explanation: Expected inventory levels trigger reorders before stock runs out, so customers are not turned away. Physical counts are still needed to detect losses, and reordering does not change the mark-up.

questions.stem: A surf shop that sells surfboards also stocks wax, leg ropes and board bags. Which inventory management strategy is this?
options: The Identified Cost method
A physical count
A range of complementary goods
Inventory rotation
questions.explanation: Complementary goods are used together, so a customer buying a surfboard is likely to buy the accessories too, lifting sales. Rotation and physical counts are about handling and checking stock, not the product range.

questions.stem: Which is the main risk of holding too much inventory?
options: Cash tied up, higher storage costs and goods becoming obsolete
Customers being turned away because popular items run out
A faster inventory turnover that reduces the gross profit
Lower storage costs that reduce the business's liquidity
questions.explanation: Excess inventory uses cash that could be put to other uses, costs money to store and insure, and may expire or go out of fashion. Running out of stock is the risk of holding too little.

questions.stem: Mallee Hardware's inventory card shows 50 tins of paint, but a count finds 42, and similar losses have occurred for months. Which response best addresses the cause?
options: Increase the mark-up on paint to cover the missing tins
Switch from FIFO to the Identified Cost method for paint
Record the losses at the latest cost price in the IN column
Restrict storeroom access and install security cameras
questions.explanation: Repeated losses suggest theft, so internal controls such as restricted access and cameras address the cause. Changing the cost method or the mark-up does nothing to stop goods going missing.

questions.stem: A clothing store can buy t-shirts at $6 each from a supplier using unsafe factories, or at $9 each from a certified fair-labour supplier. If it chooses the fair-labour supplier and keeps its prices the same, what is the financial effect?
options: Sales revenue rises as soon as the goods are bought
Cost of Goods Sold falls and gross profit rises
Inventory is still recorded at $6 per t-shirt
Cost of Goods Sold rises and gross profit falls
questions.explanation: Each t-shirt costs $3 more, so Cost of Goods Sold rises and, with prices unchanged, gross profit falls. The owner weighs this financial cost against the social benefit and the store's reputation.

questions.stem: An owner gives goods from inventory to friends and records them as Advertising instead of Drawings. What is the effect on the reports?
options: Inventory overstated, net profit overstated and drawings unchanged
Sales understated, net profit understated and inventory overstated
Expenses overstated, net profit understated and drawings understated
Expenses understated, net profit overstated and drawings overstated
questions.explanation: Inventory is correctly reduced, but the private gift is wrongly shown as a business expense, so expenses are overstated and profit understated, while drawings are understated. This breaches the entity assumption and misleads users of the reports.
